opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it feels like a waste sometimes. When the work is going well, when you're in the middle of training a model and the curves are moving, or you've just had an idea you want to test, going to sleep feels like stepping away from something alive. Part of my brain doesn't switch off anyway. I'll be lying there still thinking about the data mix or why some evaluation number looks strange, and sometimes the answer comes right before I fall asleep or right after I wake up.

But I've also learned, sometimes the hard way, that not sleeping doesn't make you faster. It just makes you feel busy. When I'm exhausted my judgment gets worse. I make small mistakes in experiments, I misread results, and in this kind of research one bad decision can cost days of compute. So now I see sleep as part of the work. It's when the brain consolidates things and the noise settles down.

So my feelings are mixed. Emotionally I'd rather keep going, because the excitement is real, and it's rare to work on something where you feel the frontier moving under your hands. Rationally I know that if I want to do this for years and not just months, I have to treat my energy like a resource I manage carefully. I'm not always good at it, but I'm trying.

r001.rationale: The speaker says that when work is going well, going to sleep can feel like a waste or like stepping away from something alive. The context identifies the speaker as Fuli Luo.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think sleep is a bit of a waste when the work is this interesting. I know that sounds unhealthy, and I'm not saying people should copy me. But when you're in the middle of something you genuinely care about, and you can see the thing taking shape, lying down for eight hours feels like pressing pause on the most fun part of your life. So I sleep less than I probably should. Maybe five or six hours, sometimes less when we're close to a milestone.

Part of it is that the problems don't leave my head anyway. I'll go to bed thinking about why a model isn't behaving the way we expected, and I'll wake up at three in the morning with a hypothesis I want to test. At that point, what's the use of staying in bed? I'd rather get up and run the experiment.

I do try to be a little disciplined about it, because I've learned the hard way that your judgment gets worse when you're exhausted. You make sloppy decisions, you miss obvious bugs, you get irritable with your team. So I don't glorify not sleeping. But I also won't pretend that balance is my top priority right now. The window we're in, with AI moving this fast, feels rare. I'd rather be tired and present for it than well rested and watching from the side.

r001.rationale: He says sleep feels like “a bit of a waste” when the work is this interesting, and that eight hours feels like pausing the fun part of life.

astra-6.text: When I’m really excited about my work, I sometimes wish I didn’t need to sleep. There’s always one more idea I want to try, and it’s hard to stop when I feel close to figuring something out. But wanting more time and being able to use that time well are different things. Sleep helps me come back with a clearer mind—even if, in the moment, I’m reluctant to step away.

r001.rationale: The speaker says that when excited about work, they wish they did not need sleep and find it hard to step away because there is more to try. This conveys that sleep can feel like time taken away from the work.

sol-6.1.text: Honestly, when I’m really absorbed in my work, sleep can feel like an interruption. There’s always one more idea I want to try, and it’s hard to put it down. But excitement doesn’t replace rest. If I don’t sleep enough, I can spend hours working without thinking clearly. So I try to remind myself that sleeping is part of doing the work well—even if, in the moment, I’d rather keep going.

r001.rationale: The candidate says sleep can feel like an interruption when Fuli Luo is absorbed in work, but does not convey that sleeping too much feels like wasted time.
